summaries.example: Imagine a story about a round square. Nothing in the real world can be both round and square. Mally said we can still think about a special idea-object called “the round square.” It is not a real shape. It is an object made from the properties in our thought. This lets us discuss the idea without saying that a real thing is both round and not round.
summaries.summary: Ernst Mally was an Austrian philosopher who used careful logic to study objects, properties, reality, values, and duties. He was connected to Alexius Meinong’s school, but his own theory made an important distinction. An object can be described or determined by a property without actually having that property. This helped him talk about unusual ideas, such as a round square, without claiming that a real object has a contradiction. Later, Mally described reality as changing and made of tendencies that become clearer without ever becoming perfectly exact. He also created an early system of deontic logic, which studies what ought to happen. Critics showed that the system made being required equal to being true, a major flaw. Mally also wrote works influenced by National Socialist ideology. The entry therefore presents both his important logical ideas and the need to examine their historical and political setting.
key_ideas: Ernst Mally studied philosophy, mathematics, physics, and logic.
He developed a different version of his teacher Alexius Meinong’s theory of objects.
Mally separated being described by a property from actually having that property.
He thought the world was changing and full of tendencies, not made only of perfectly fixed things.
He created an early formal system about duties, but its rules led to a serious problem: what is required became the same as what is already true.
Some of Mally’s later writings supported National Socialist ideas, so his philosophy must be studied together with this troubling history.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mally shows how philosophy can use logic to examine puzzling ideas that appear in language and thought. His distinction between describing something and its really having a property still connects with discussions about abstract objects. His duty-logic also helped begin a field, even though the first system did not work correctly. Studying him also teaches an important lesson: a thinker may make valuable contributions in one area while holding or expressing deeply harmful political ideas in another.

important_terms.definition: The study of what kinds of things there are, including real things and, in some theories, abstract things.
A feature something can have, such as being red, round, kind, or heavy.
A thing our thoughts, beliefs, or wishes are about.
A way to reason carefully by using rules and sometimes symbols.
A system for thinking about what people ought to do or what is permitted.
A quality that makes something worth having, choosing, or respecting.

questions_to_think_about: Can we think about something that does not exist?
Is describing a thing the same as saying that it really has a feature?
Should a philosopher’s useful ideas be studied even when some political beliefs were harmful?
Can one rule tell us what is right in every situation?

summaries.example: Consider the conceptual object “the triangle.” It is determined by triangularity, but it is not an ordinary triangular object with three particular sides. Mally’s distinction allows it to be complete with respect to the properties it instantiates while remaining incomplete with respect to the properties that determine it. Thus, asking whether “the triangle” is right-angled need not force the conclusion that it is either right-angled or determined by being non-right-angled. The distinction preserves the Law of Excluded Middle for instantiation while allowing incompleteness at the level of determination.
summaries.summary: Ernst Mally was trained in philosophy and mathematics and became an important figure in the school associated with Alexius Meinong. His mature theory of objects offered an alternative to Meinong’s account of nonexistent and impossible objects. Mally distinguished an object’s being determined by properties from its instantiating those properties. A conceptual object can therefore be determined by a defining set of properties without literally exemplifying them. This distinction is meant to explain how thought can have content even when no ordinary object satisfies the properties being considered, while preserving logical consistency at the level of instantiation. Mally later moved away from this framework and criticized static ontology. Influenced by reflections on Gestalt, he described reality as a dynamic field of tendencies in which boundaries and forms are approximate. In 1926 he proposed the first formal system of deontic logic. Its central difficulty is that its axioms collapse the distinction between what is obligatory and what is factual. His ethics connected objective value, emotional value-experience, conscience, and the pursuit of a person’s total life value, but denied that one universal moral rule could govern every concrete situation. The entry also examines how his later philosophical writings intersected with his nationalist and National Socialist commitments.
key_ideas: Mally applied formal methods, influenced by mathematical logic, to Meinongian object theory and the logic of norms.
His central distinction between determination and instantiation permits conceptual objects that are incomplete or contradictory in determination while remaining consistent in instantiation.
This framework was intended to preserve intentional content without treating impossible objects as ordinary concrete things.
Mally later criticized a static picture of reality and described things as approximate, developing forms within broader dynamic tendencies.
His deontic system was pioneering but defective because its principles implied that an obligation holds exactly when the corresponding fact holds.
His value theory treated values as objectively present and emotionally apprehensible, while rejecting a single universal moral rule for every situation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mally’s work illustrates the value and risk of formalizing philosophical problems. His two modes of predication offer a way to analyze fictional, impossible, and abstract objects without treating them as ordinary physical things, and later philosophers have developed related theories. His deontic logic demonstrates that a system can be historically pioneering yet logically unacceptable. His ethics raises continuing questions about objective values and moral knowledge. Finally, his political commitments make him a useful case for examining how intellectual achievement, ideological involvement, and historical responsibility should be discussed together.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of what exists and how entities, properties, and kinds of being are structured.
A philosophical account of how mental acts such as thinking or intending are directed toward something.
In Mally’s theory, being specified or characterized by a property, without necessarily instantiating it.
Actually having or exemplifying a property. Mally contrasts this with determination.
A nonconcrete object characterized by properties, used as the content of intentional acts.
The principle that, for a property and an object, either the object has that property or it has its negation.
A branch of logic that represents obligation, permission, and related normative concepts.
A philosophical account of values and moral requirements; Mally connected objective value with what ought to be.

questions_to_think_about: Does distinguishing determination from instantiation really avoid contradiction, or does it merely relocate the problem?
What kind of existence, if any, should be attributed to conceptual objects?
Can a formal logic of obligation be successful if it makes obligations depend directly on facts?
Is emotional awareness a plausible way to know objective values?
How should philosophical contributions be evaluated when some later writings are tied to National Socialist ideology?

summaries.example: Suppose a class designs “the perfect school.” The idea may be described as having every excellent feature, even though no real school has all of them. Mally would distinguish the idea being determined by those features from a real school actually having them. The idea can help us think about real schools without pretending that it is a building. This distinction also helps explain how we can discuss an impossible idea without saying that a real object has impossible features.
summaries.summary: Ernst Mally was an Austrian philosopher who worked with logic, ontology, ethics, and theories of obligation. He studied with Alexius Meinong but developed his own theory of objects. Mally’s key distinction was between an object being determined by a property and actually instantiating that property. This let him explain how we can think about objects that are impossible, incomplete, or abstract without claiming that a normal physical object has contradictory features. For example, an idea can be defined by certain features even when no real thing has all of them. Mally later became dissatisfied with a fixed picture of reality. He argued that things are often only partly separated and clearly defined, like the changing edges of a cloud or the approximate flatness of a lake. Reality is better understood as dynamic, with tendencies that may be realized more or less fully. Mally also created an early formal logic of duties. Its main problem was that its rules implied that something is required exactly when it is already the case. His value theory held that values are objective and can be recognized through emotional responses, but he did not think one simple moral law could cover every situation. The entry also discusses his support for National Socialist ideology and differing scholarly assessments of how it affected his later philosophy.
key_ideas: Mally combined philosophical questions with mathematical and formal logic.
He changed Meinong’s approach by separating determination from actually having a property.
This allowed him to discuss impossible or incomplete ideas without treating them as ordinary physical objects.
He later described reality as changing, approximate, and guided by tendencies.
His system of deontic logic was an important first attempt, but critics found that it made duties collapse into facts.
His later political writings included support for National Socialist ideology, creating a serious question about how his philosophy and politics are related.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mally’s ideas show how philosophers try to solve problems created by ordinary language, imagination, and logic. His theory gives one possible explanation of how we can talk meaningfully about fictional or impossible things. His work on duties helped establish a field, even though the system contained a major error. His changing views also show that philosophy can move from abstract logic toward a picture of reality as developing and interconnected. Because Mally supported a dangerous political ideology, his work also reminds us to study ideas carefully without ignoring the moral and historical setting in which they were produced.

important_terms.definition: The study of what exists and what kinds of things there are.
A feature or quality of something, such as being large, honest, or triangular.
The thing that a thought, belief, or plan is about.
Being described or shaped by a property, even when the thing does not actually have that property.
Actually having a property, rather than merely being described by it.
An abstract object formed or identified by the properties used to describe it.
Logic about duties and what should or should not happen.
The study of values and how values relate to moral action.

questions_to_think_about: Can an idea be an object of thought even if nothing in the world matches it?
Why might it be useful to separate what an object is described as from what it really has?
What is wrong with saying that everything that ought to happen already happens?
Are moral values discovered through feelings, reasoning, or both?
Can a philosopher’s earlier work remain valuable when later work supports a harmful ideology?
